jobs.title: Lit, then shut off every few seconds

jobs.title: Hummed, then stopped before lighting

items.question: Will your repair affect my American Standard warranty?
items.answer: No. American Standard covers the parts. We fit genuine parts, check your registration by serial number and file the claim, so a covered part costs you labor only.

items.question: Where do I find my American Standard model number?
items.answer: On the rating plate inside the lower door, near the blower. Read us the model and serial number when you call and we'll bring the right parts.

items.question: Why is my American Standard furnace blinking red?
items.answer: The light is a fault code. Tell us how many times it flashes when you call, and our technician brings the parts for that fault.

items.question: Is it worth repairing a 15-year-old furnace?
items.answer: Often yes for an ignitor, sensor or switch. We put the repair and replacement numbers side by side, check the heat exchanger, and you decide.

items.question: How fast can you come when there's no heat?
items.answer: We answer 24/7, and a no-heat call goes to the front of the line for a same-day visit.

parts.h2: Every part of your American Standard furnace we look after
parts.note: Prices from citysuburbanheating.com and City of Chicago permits. Terms and conditions apply.

items.title: Hot-surface ignitor
items.body: The part that glows to light the gas. A cracked one is the most common reason a furnace won’t start.

items.title: Flame sensor
items.body: A small rod that proves the flame is lit. When it’s coated, the burners light, then shut off.

items.title: Inducer motor
items.body: The fan that clears the exhaust before the burners light. A loud hum or rattle often starts here.
ticks: Matched to your model and serial number

items.title: Pressure switch
items.body: Proves the exhaust is flowing. A blocked vent or drain trips it, and the furnace stops.
ticks: Tested along with the vent and drain

items.title: Control board
items.body: The furnace’s brain. Its status light flashes a code that tells us where to look.
ticks: Tested on our meter before we replace it
Flash code read on every visit

items.title: Blower motor
items.body: Moves warm air through your ducts. On Gold and Platinum models it changes speed.
ticks: Checked for current draw and bearing noise
Variable-speed motors matched to the model

items.title: Gas valve
items.body: Lets gas into the burners. On the Platinum 95 it turns the flame up and down in small steps.
ticks: Gas pressure measured on every visit

items.title: Heat exchanger
items.body: Keeps the flame and exhaust apart from the air you breathe. A crack means the furnace has to be shut off.
ticks: Inspected and CO tested at every tune-up

items.title: Venting
items.body: The PVC pipes on a 95% furnace, or the chimney liner on an 80% one, carry the exhaust safely outside.
ticks: Checked for draft and leaks on every visit

sizing.h2: Decide how much house your furnace has to heat
sizing.calloutTitle: A furnace only heats evenly when it’s sized to the house.
sizing.calloutBody: Too small and the far rooms stay cold on the worst nights. Too big and it short cycles, wears out sooner and leaves the house uneven. We size it room by room, not by the old furnace’s label.
sizing.note: What decides the size: the rooms and floors, the windows and insulation, the ducts, and how cold the coldest Chicago night gets.

scenarios.title: A condo or flat
scenarios.body: One level with shared walls: a smaller, often single-stage furnace keeps it warm without short cycling.

scenarios.title: A bungalow
scenarios.body: A main floor plus a finished basement or attic: a two-stage furnace runs low most days and steps up in a cold snap.

scenarios.title: A two-flat or a bigger home
scenarios.body: More floors and more rooms: a larger or modulating furnace, sometimes one per unit, with the ducts checked so the top floor gets its share.

estimateChecks.h2: What we check before we quote

checks.title: Where the furnace sits
checks.body: Room around it for service, and the clearances American Standard’s install manual asks for.

checks.title: Your gas line and meter
checks.body: The gas line size and pressure, so the new furnace gets all the gas it needs.

checks.title: Venting and chimney
checks.body: A 95% furnace vents in PVC through the wall; an 80% one needs a sound, lined chimney.

checks.title: Your ductwork
checks.body: Supply and return ducts big enough for the airflow, with no crushed runs or missing returns.

checks.title: Heat exchanger and CO
checks.body: On the old furnace, a crack or high carbon monoxide means it can’t stay in service.

checks.title: The size your home needs
checks.body: Rooms, floors, windows and insulation, measured, not copied from the old furnace.

checks.title: Your thermostat
checks.body: Whether it suits a two-stage or modulating furnace, or needs replacing too.

checks.title: The condensate drain
checks.body: A 95% furnace makes water, so it needs a drain or a pump that won’t freeze.

checks.title: Filter and air quality
checks.body: The filter size and fit, and whether a humidifier or air cleaner belongs on the new furnace.

checks.title: An American Standard you already have
checks.body: For repairs: the model and serial number, its age, the flash code and its service history.

estimateChecks.routesHeading: If your chimney can’t vent the new furnace

routes.title: The chimney is lined and sound
routes.body: An 80% furnace connects to the existing liner. No chimney work.

routes.title: The chimney is unlined or worn
routes.body: A new liner goes in first, so exhaust can’t leak back into the house.

routes.title: Skip the chimney
routes.body: A 95% furnace vents through the wall in PVC, so the old chimney isn’t needed.

estimateChecks.routesNote: Which route fits is decided at the visit, before any work starts.

sections.title: Furnaces, boilers and gas
sections.body: 335,769 properties heat with a warm-air furnace and 98,849 with hot water or steam. A furnace is the most common heat in the city, and most of them burn natural gas, which is why gas pressure and venting are checked on every visit.

sections.title: Basements and chimneys
sections.body: Most furnaces sit in the basement: 324,305 properties have a full one. In older brick homes the furnace often vents up a chimney built long before modern furnaces, so the liner gets checked before a new 80% furnace is connected to it.

sections.title: The Chicago Heat Ordinance
sections.body: From September 15 to June 1, rental units in Chicago must reach at least 68°F from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. and 66°F overnight. A furnace that stops in a rental is an urgent call, and we treat it that way.
